# V

V is the oldest known Riftborn — a figure who arrived through the Rift decades ago and has been searching for a way back ever since. Unlike most Riftborn, V retained memories of their original world: a place V describes only as "green" and "quiet" and "gone." Those three words are the most personal information V has ever shared about themself.

V founded the Returners not as an army but as a support network — Riftborn helping Riftborn, pooling knowledge and resources toward a shared goal. Over the decades, the Returners grew into something larger: a research organization, a political force, and the closest thing the Severed Lands has to a Riftborn advocacy group. V didn't plan any of that. V just kept working, and people kept joining.

V is rarely at Waystation. They spend most of their time in the field — tracking leads on Warden fragments, investigating the two unaccounted-for Doors, following Rift surge patterns that might reveal something about the Doors' decline. When V returns, decisions get made. When V is gone, the senior Returners keep things running.

## Personality

V is patient, methodical, and carrying the weight of decades. They don't inspire through charisma — they inspire through competence. Every Returner knows that V has given their entire life to this mission. That kind of commitment is hard to argue with, and V rarely needs to argue.

V is not cold, but they are guarded. They've lost too many people — Returners who died on patrol, Riftborn who gave up and left, friends who became Hollowed and stopped recognizing them. V doesn't form new attachments easily. When they do, it's significant.

V's defining trait is patience bordering on obsession. They've been working on the Door problem for longer than most Returners have been alive. They believe the answer exists — in a Warden inscription they haven't found yet, in a Door fragment they haven't recovered, in a surge pattern they haven't mapped. The belief is not faith. It's the conclusion of decades of evidence. V is not guessing. V is waiting.

## Role in a Campaign

**As ally:** V is the quest-giver, the mentor, the voice of experience. They send the party after Warden fragments, Door leads, and Rift surge data. They provide context, resources, and the occasional warning that goes unheeded until it's too late.

**As antagonist:** V's patience has a dark side. If the party discovers a way to force the Door open — a method V considers too dangerous, too uncertain, too likely to bring something through first — V will oppose them. Not with violence. V doesn't do violence. But with obstruction, with withheld information, with the full weight of the Returners' loyalty. The party wants to force the Door. V has spent decades trying to open it safely. Neither side is wrong. The conflict writes itself.

**As mystery:** V knows more than they share. About their home world. About the Wardens. About what they've seen in the deep Cairnfields and the unaccounted-for Door sites. A campaign that earns V's trust might eventually learn the full story. A campaign that doesn't might never know what V was really looking for.

## Behind the Screen

V's true nature is left deliberately ambiguous. Possible truths include:

- V is exactly what they appear to be: a Riftborn who remembers home and wants to return.
- V was part of the Wardens — not metaphorically, literally. V's "decades" of searching might be centuries. The Wardens' symbol — a circle bisected by a line — appears in V's personal notes.
- V knows why the Doors are dying. They're not trying to open the Door. They're trying to prevent something from coming through.
- V's home world was destroyed by whatever created the Rift. V isn't trying to go home. V is trying to make sure it doesn't happen here.

The truth is for the DM to decide. The ambiguity is the point.

# Old Crane

Old Crane is the oldest living practitioner of the Veiled Path — a monk who's been living at the Spire, the tallest pillar in the Cairnfields, for longer than anyone can verify. He claims sixty years. He looks older. Some of his stories reference events that happened eighty years ago. When asked about the discrepancy, he says the Veil confuses time. He says it with the kind of casual certainty that's hard to argue with.

Crane no longer trains students. He lives at the Spire in solitude, trading information for supplies with Returner patrols and the occasional brave scavenger. He knows the Cairnfields better than anyone — every pillar, every pool, every riftbeast territory. He's seen things in the Veil that he won't describe. When the Returners signal him and he signals back, it's usually bad news.

Crane's body has been partially transformed by decades of phase-stepping — his movements are slightly out of sync with his physical position, like a video that's a frame behind. His voice echoes even when there's nothing to echo off. He's more Veil than flesh at this point. He seems fine with it.

## Personality

Crane is distant, amused, and evasive when asked direct questions. He speaks in fragments that feel like koans but might just be the Veil's influence on his syntax. He's not hostile — he genuinely seems to enjoy visitors — but he's been alone for so long that conversation is a skill he's half-forgotten. He treats urgency like a mild curiosity. Nothing in the Cairnfields is urgent. Urgency is a surface-world concept.

## Hook

Crane is signaling Waystation — three mirrored flashes, the emergency code. He hasn't signaled in years. The last time he did, a Rift surge reshaped the eastern Cairnfields. Whatever he's seen from the Spire, it's worse.

# Iro

Iro is a Rift Seeker — a descendant of the Rift Raiders who rejected the martial code and sought inner stillness instead. He's been wandering the Cairnfields for fifteen years, mastering the discipline that his ancestors considered cowardice. He's not a coward. He's just decided that the Eternal Battle his people believe in isn't a war. It's the struggle to stay calm in a world that wants you to fight.

Iro occasionally serves as a translator between the Raiders and outsiders — one of the few people who speaks both Rift-tongue and Common, and the only one the Raiders will tolerate. He doesn't enjoy it. Translating for Korr means listening to Korr's plans and being unable to warn anyone. Translating for Vex means standing in silence for hours while she writes orders that will get people killed. The Seeker's discipline is non-interference. The discipline is very hard to maintain.

## Personality

Iro is calm, melancholy, and carrying the weight of his people's choices. He loves the Raiders. They're his family, his heritage, his blood. He also believes they're wrong — about the Eternal Battle, about violence as purpose, about everything. He can't change them. He can barely stand to watch. But he stays, because someone has to speak for them, and he's the only one who can.

# Tessa

Tessa runs the best bakery in Thornwall. Her bread is the reason the morning market has a line before sunrise. She's been baking since she could reach the oven — her mother ran the bakery before her, and her grandmother before that. The recipes haven't changed in three generations. The quality hasn't either.

Tessa doesn't care about Riftborn politics. She cares about flour prices. The council's grain tariffs — controlled by House Voss — directly affect her margins. She's been quietly vocal about this at market gatherings. "Quietly vocal" in Thornwall means she says things that sound like complaints about the weather but everyone knows are complaints about Lord Voss.

She'll sell to anyone. She'll also slip an extra roll to the Warrens kids who hang around the market at closing time. She doesn't make a thing of it. The rolls just happen to be "leftover."

## Personality

Warm, practical, and politically aware in the way that small business owners have to be. Tessa treats baking as craft and community — the bakery feeds Thornwall, and Thornwall takes care of the bakery. That's how it's always worked. She doesn't see why Riftborn should be any different.

# Auntie Salt

Auntie Salt runs the Warrens' information network — a web of barkeeps, merchants, street kids, and domestic servants who feed her everything they see and hear. She's the Warrens Court's intelligence arm, but she's not loyal to the Court. She's loyal to the information trade, and she sells to anyone who can pay.

Salt has no territory and no gang. Her currency is knowledge, and she's the richest person in the Warrens — not in gold, but in leverage. She knows about Kael's daughter. She knows about Trask's Nexus negotiations. She knows which Warrens resident has been cultivating a Rift pool in their basement. She's known that last one for weeks. She hasn't told anyone yet. She's waiting for the right buyer.

Salt's network extends beyond the Warrens — she has informants in Thornwall proper, in the Hollows Crews, and (rumor has it) in the Athenaeum. The extent of her reach is unknown. The accuracy of her information is frighteningly consistent.

## Personality

Salt is cheerful, grandmotherly, and utterly amoral about the information trade. She treats secrets like produce — some are fresh, some are past their sell-by date, all of them have a price. She genuinely likes people. She just likes knowing things about them more. She keeps a pot of tea going at all hours. Visitors are always offered a cup. No one knows if the tea is safe. Fume sells alchemical supplies in the Crossroads market — reagents and the occasional Rift-touched compound that the Athenaeum would classify as hazardous. Saffron runs a herbalist stall in the Thornwall market by day and a free clinic in the Warrens by night. # The Lace Brothers

They specialize in contraband the Thornwall Council has banned: unsanctioned Warden fragments, Rift-touched curios, information that would get someone killed if it reached the right ears.

They're the Warrens' primary link to the Hollows Crews — every crew that pulls something valuable out of the ruins eventually does business with the Lace Brothers. They're also the primary fence for the Caravan Jackals, which the Court officially doesn't know about and unofficially profits from.

The Brothers are ambitious, young, and already eyeing Madame Thistle's territory. When Thistle dies — and she is dying — the succession fight will be between the Brothers and Thistle's lieutenants. The Brothers have been preparing. They've been stockpiling funds, building alliances, and making the kind of promises that are very hard to break.

## Personality

The Brothers present a unified front but have distinct personalities: Thread is the negotiator — smooth, charming, always smiling. Hook is the enforcer — quiet, watchful, never more than arm's reach from a weapon. Needle is the logistics mind — the one who knows where everything is, who owes what, whose shipment is late. They finish each other's sentences. It's unsettling.

The Brothers have acquired something unusual — a Warden artifact that's fully intact, not fragmentary. They're not sure what it does. They're auctioning it to the highest bidder. The Returners, House Kael, and the Unbound are all bidding. The Brothers are drawing out the auction. They're enjoying the attention.

# Drum

Drum is a fence — he buys scavenged goods from independent scavengers who don't want to deal with the Lace Brothers' commission rates. His operation is smaller, quieter, and considerably less legal than the Brothers'. The Court tolerates him because he handles the volume they don't want. The council doesn't know he exists. Drum prefers it that way.

Drum's specialty is items that are too hot for the regular market — artifacts with identifiable origins, goods that "fell off a caravan," information that would start a war if it reached the wrong faction. He doesn't ask where things come from. He doesn't share who he sells to. His operation is built on the principle that the less you know, the less you can be forced to reveal.

## Personality

Drum is nervous, meticulous, and very good at staying invisible. He treats fencing as a risk management profession — every transaction is calculated, every buyer is vetted, every item is stored in a different location. He's been doing this for years. He's never been caught. He intends to keep it that way.

# Soot

Soot is Thornwall's ratcatcher — a profession that sounds humble but involves more knowledge of the city's infrastructure than anyone except Grim. He knows every drain, every basement access, every forgotten passage between the market and the Warrens. He's been doing this job for fifteen years. He's very good at it. The rats are not.

Soot is also the Warrens' unofficial supply line. He carries messages, medicine, and the occasional small package between the surface and the underground. The guards don't search the ratcatcher. No one wants to search the ratcatcher. Soot uses this to his advantage.

He doesn't charge for the deliveries. He just does them. Someone helped him once — a Riftborn in the Warrens, years ago, when he was sick and couldn't work. He's been paying it forward ever since. The Warrens knows him by smell — the rats follow him, and the residents know to step aside.

## Personality

Soot is quiet, grimy, and more connected than anyone realizes. He treats his work as a calling rather than a job. The rats are part of the city. The Warrens is part of the city. Soot takes care of both.

# Corin

Corin runs Thornwall's caravan yard — the stables, the wagon repairs, the organized chaos of a commercial hub's logistics. He's been a stablemaster for twenty-five years. He's forgotten more about horses than most people will ever know. He's also one of the few settled humans who regularly interacts with animals from other worlds — some Riftborn arrived with mounts, and those mounts sometimes bred.

Corin doesn't care about Riftborn politics. He cares about animals. A Riftborn with a sick horse gets the same treatment as a Thornwall merchant with a lame mule. The animals don't know about registration requirements. They just need care. Corin provides it.

# Echo

Echo is a bard of the College of Echoes — a subclass that channels fragments of lost worlds through song. Their performances aren't entertainment. They're remembrance. When Echo sings, the audience hears snatches of music from home worlds they can't return to, melodies from places that might not exist anymore, harmonies that feel like memory even to people who remember nothing.

Echo travels between settlements — Waystation, Thornwall, Nexus, the smaller villages that the Guild caravans serve. They perform in taverns and market squares, never charging, never staying long. People who hear Echo's songs sometimes cry without knowing why. Sometimes they remember things they'd forgotten. Sometimes they ask Echo to stop. Echo always stops.

The College of Echoes teaches that music is the only thing that crosses the Rift unchanged. Echo believes this. They're not sure if it's a blessing or a curse.

# Fume

Fume sells alchemical supplies in the Crossroads market — reagents and the occasional Rift-touched compound that the Athenaeum would classify as hazardous. He arrived through the Rift with a case of alchemical formulas and the burns to prove he'd tested most of them. His stall smells of sulfur and something sweeter that lingers in the sinuses.

Fume is the go-to for anyone who needs something unstable. Returner patrols buy his Rift-burn salve. Hollows scavengers buy his glow-paste — a compound that emits light for hours without heat, essential for navigating the ruins without attracting riftbeasts. The Athenaeum buys his more exotic compounds through intermediaries. Fume doesn't ask what they're for. He just provides the materials.

# Kestrel

Kestrel runs the Crossroads auction — the weekly event where the most valuable salvage, artifacts, and curiosities find their buyers. She's been an auctioneer for twelve years. Her voice carries across the entire market. Her memory for bids, buyers, and debts is flawless. She's never had to call a bid twice.

She knows which items are stolen, which are fake, and which are dangerous. She doesn't announce any of this. She just sets the starting price accordingly. A fake goes low. A dangerous item goes high — if someone's going to take a risk, they're going to pay for it.

# Drum

Drum is a fence — he buys scavenged goods from independent scavengers who don't want to deal with the Lace Brothers' commission rates. His operation is smaller, quieter, and considerably less legal than the Brothers'. The Court tolerates him because he handles the volume they don't want. The council doesn't know he exists. Drum prefers it that way.

Drum's specialty is items that are too hot for the regular market — artifacts with identifiable origins, goods that "fell off a caravan," information that would start a war if it reached the wrong faction. He doesn't ask where things come from. He doesn't share who he sells to. His operation is built on the principle that the less you know, the less you can be forced to reveal.

## Personality

Drum is nervous, meticulous, and very good at staying invisible. He treats fencing as a risk management profession — every transaction is calculated, every buyer is vetted, every item is stored in a different location. He's been doing this for years. # Soot

Soot is Thornwall's ratcatcher — a profession that sounds humble but involves more knowledge of the city's infrastructure than anyone except Grim. He knows every drain, every basement access, every forgotten passage between the market and the Warrens. He's been doing this job for fifteen years. He's very good at it. The rats are not.

Soot is also the Warrens' unofficial supply line. He carries messages, medicine, and the occasional small package between the surface and the underground. The guards don't search the ratcatcher. No one wants to search the ratcatcher. Soot uses this to his advantage.

He doesn't charge for the deliveries. He just does them. Someone helped him once — a Riftborn in the Warrens, years ago, when he was sick and couldn't work. He's been paying it forward ever since. The Warrens knows him by smell — the rats follow him, and the residents know to step aside.

Soot is quiet, grimy, and more connected than anyone realizes. He treats his work as a calling rather than a job. The rats are part of the city. The Warrens is part of the city. Soot takes care of both.

# Corin

Corin runs Thornwall's caravan yard — the stables, the wagon repairs, the organized chaos of a commercial hub's logistics. He's been a stablemaster for twenty-five years. He's forgotten more about horses than most people will ever know. He's also one of the few settled humans who regularly interacts with animals from other worlds — some Riftborn arrived with mounts, and those mounts sometimes bred.

Corin doesn't care about Riftborn politics. He cares about animals. A Riftborn with a sick horse gets the same treatment as a Thornwall merchant with a lame mule. The animals don't know about registration requirements. They just need care. Corin provides it.

He's also the Guild's unofficial veterinarian — caravan animals that get injured on the routes come to Corin. He's saved more Guild livelihoods than the Route Warden. He'd never say so out loud.

## Personality

Corin is gruff, gentle with animals, and allergic to politics. He treats every creature that comes through his yard the same: assess the problem, fix the problem, send them on their way. The world would be simpler if people were more like horses.

She's one of the few market vendors who'll take Riftborn commissions without the usual markup or hesitation. Clothes are clothes. Bodies are bodies. Lace has measured every shape that walks through Thornwall's gates, and she's never found one that didn't deserve to be warm.

Her shop is small — two rooms above the market, fabric bolts stacked to the ceiling. She works by candlelight. She hums while she sews. The tune is from a world she's never visited, learned from a Riftborn customer who couldn't remember where it came from. Lace remembers.

# Miri

Miri is a gate guard — one of the men and women who check everyone entering Thornwall. She's been on gate duty for three years. She's seen every kind of arrival: merchants with caravans, Returners with supply requests, Riftborn with hope and fear in equal measure.

Miri processes Riftborn registrations by the book — name, origin if known, purpose of visit. She asks the required questions. She doesn't ask the ones the book doesn't require. A Riftborn who stammers on the "origin" question gets a moment to collect themselves. A Riftborn who looks like they haven't eaten gets directions to the Warrens. Miri doesn't break policy. She just administers it with the most humanity the policy allows.

Her brother was Riftborn — arrived ten years ago, no memories, died in a Hollows scavenging accident before Miri ever got to know him. She wears his ring on a chain under her uniform. She doesn't talk about it.

## Personality

Quiet, dutiful, and carrying a private grief. Miri does her job. She doesn't make waves. She just makes sure the Gate is slightly less terrifying than it could be.

An adult Human woman in her early thirties with an athletic lean build, deep warm brown skin, dark brown eyes, a long oval face and tightly braided dark hair gathered behind her head. Plain muted blue-gray guard tunic, closed collar, practical steel mail shirt under a simple dark leather jerkin, dark trousers, brown boots, plain belt and sheathed short sidearm. # Madame Thistle

Madame Thistle is the Warrens' oldest boss and its closest thing to a legitimate leader. She controls the northern quarter — the densest residential area — and runs protection rackets like an insurance policy. Pay regularly, and problems disappear. Refuse to pay, and you're on your own. Thistle's operation is less a criminal enterprise than a municipal government with a flexible tax structure.

She arrived through the Rift forty years ago — before the Returners existed, before the Warrens was the Warrens, when Thornwall was still deciding whether Riftborn were guests or threats. She's been here longer than most settled families. She's outlasted three council compositions, two Warrens gang wars, and one attempted council crackdown that ended with the guards refusing to enter the northern quarter. The council has quietly approached her more than once about "managing the Riftborn situation." She listens. She doesn't commit.

Thistle is dying. She's been dying for a year — something in her lungs, a Rift-touched condition that the Athenaeum's healers can't identify. She's been grooming a successor, but the Lace Brothers are circling, and the succession fight is going to be bloody.

## Personality

Thistle is tired, amused, and too old to be intimidated. She speaks slowly, as if each word costs her something. She's forgotten more about the Warrens than most people will ever know. She genuinely cares about her territory — not as a source of income, but as a community she's spent forty years building. The protection money funds street repairs, dispute resolution, and the Warrens' unofficial orphanage. "Taxation with representation," she calls it. "Just not the council's representation."

## Hook

Thistle is ready to name her successor — but she wants something first. A Rift pool in the northern quarter, hidden in a basement, cultivated by someone she can't identify. She wants it found and destroyed before she dies. She's offering her endorsement — and her territory's loyalty — to whoever helps.

# Grim

Grim controls the tunnels — the warren-passages that connect the Thornwall Warrens to the market district above, the city's underbelly, and (if the rumors are true) the Undercroft beneath Nexus. He doesn't run a gang. He runs a toll system. Pay, and you pass. Don't pay, and you don't get to use his tunnels twice.

Grim is neutral in Warrens Court politics. His tunnels are too valuable for anyone to challenge him — every faction in the Warrens depends on his routes. The Lace Brothers move contraband through his passages. Madame Thistle's protection runners use them to avoid guard patrols. Auntie Salt's informants use them to move unseen. Grim charges everyone the same rate and favors no one.

He's also the Warrens' unofficial cartographer — he knows the tunnels better than anyone, including the ones that predate the Warrens, the ones that were here before Thornwall was built. He doesn't share his maps. He doesn't need to. If you want to go somewhere in the Warrens, you go through Grim, or you don't go.

## Personality

Grim is quiet, professional, and completely uninterested in anything that doesn't involve his tunnels. He treats passage rights like a business — fair rates, consistent enforcement, no exceptions. He's not friendly. He's not hostile. He's infrastructure.

# Shrike

Shrike leads the Dusk Boys — a Jackal band that specializes in night raids. Quick strikes, minimal violence, maximum confusion. Her band hits caravans that make camp after dark and melts back into the darkness before the guards can organize. They're the most efficient Jackal operation on the routes. They've never killed anyone. They've never needed to.

Shrike was a Hollows scavenger before she realized banditry had a better survival rate. She's not wrong. The Hollows killed four of her crewmates in two years. The routes haven't killed any of her Jackals — she runs her band like she ran her crew, with the same discipline and the same understanding that one mistake means someone doesn't come back.

She's been watching Gareth's unification push with interest. The Red Banner is the largest band, but Shrike has something Gareth doesn't: the respect of every smaller band on the routes. If the moot goes against Gareth, Shrike is the natural alternative. She's not sure she wants the job.

## Personality

Shrike is professional, calculating, and utterly unsentimental about her work. Banditry is a trade, not an identity. She treats it accordingly — fair rates, minimal violence, consistent results. Her raiders respect her. The merchants she hits respect her. That's rarer than it sounds.

# Lady Sera Kael

Lady Kael is the Thornwall Council's swing vote — and its most carefully guarded secret. She controls the textile and luxury goods trade, presenting herself as a pragmatist who votes with whichever side serves Kael interests. Her public persona is unremarkable: a competent merchant, a reliable council member, a woman who keeps her own counsel.

Her private persona is considerably more interesting. Lady Kael has been quietly funding Anchor Door research for years — funnelling gold through a shell trading company to the Returners, the Athenaeum, and independent scholars. She's the reason the Returners have functioning equipment. She's the reason the Athenaeum's Warden Studies school hasn't collapsed from lack of funding. She's the reason three different scavenger expeditions found Door fragments that "happened" to be exactly where her researchers predicted.

Why? Kael's eldest daughter is Riftborn. Arrived seven years ago with no memory, no home world, no explanation. Kael pulled every string to keep it quiet — registered her as a distant relative, hid her in the family estate, lied to the council for seven years. Her daughter wants to go home. Kael wants to give her that chance. Everything else — the research funding, the political maneuvering, the years of deception — serves that single goal.

## Personality

Kael is warm, measured, and impossible to read. She's spent seven years lying to the most powerful people in the Severed Lands, and she's gotten very good at it. She treats every conversation as a negotiation where the other party doesn't know the stakes.

She genuinely likes people — she's not cold or calculating in the way Lord Merrick is. She just has a priority that outweighs everything else, and she's made peace with what that costs. If the council discovered her secret, she'd be disgraced. If her daughter were exposed, she'd be in danger. Kael accepts both risks. The Door research is worth it. Her daughter is worth it.

## Role in a Campaign

**As ally:** Kael is the inside source on the Thornwall Council. She provides funding, intelligence, and political cover for Riftborn-aligned operations. She'll never admit to any of it publicly. A campaign that earns her trust gains access to resources no other Thornwall faction can match.

**As subject of exposure:** Kael's secret is a ticking bomb. If Lord Voss or Lord Merrick discovered it, the council would fracture. A campaign might protect her, expose her, or use the information as leverage. Kael would understand any of those choices. She might even help with the last one, if the exchange served her daughter's interests.

## Hook

Kael's daughter has started remembering. Fragments — a name, a color, a feeling of water. She wants to find her home world. Kael needs information that only the Returners have, and the Returners need funding that only Kael can provide. The arrangement is delicate. Something is about to break it.

# Lord Silas Merrick

Lord Merrick imports spices and alchemical supplies, but his real business is intelligence. He knows everything that happens in Thornwall and most of what happens outside it. His network includes merchants, guards, Warrens residents, at least one Returner, and a Hollowed informant deep in the Hollows who may not know they're an informant.

Merrick is the council's quietest member — he rarely speaks in sessions. When he does, the room goes still. He's not threatening. He doesn't need to be. Everyone on the council knows that Merrick has files on them — their secrets, their vulnerabilities, the things they'd pay to keep hidden. Merrick has never used any of it. The knowledge itself is the power. Using it would reduce its value.

He's not cruel. He's not kind. He's a collector. Information is the only currency that never depreciates, and Merrick has been collecting for thirty years. He knows about Kael's daughter. He knows about Trask's Nexus negotiations. He knows about Voss's dead son and the unresolved questions around the Rift surge that killed him. He knows more than anyone, and he shares less than anyone, and he sleeps fine at night.

## Personality

Merrick is soft-spoken, patient, and genuinely curious. He asks questions because he wants to know the answers — not to use them, necessarily, but because not knowing bothers him. He treats conversations like puzzles. He treats people the same way.

He's not a villain in waiting. Merrick has never blackmailed anyone, never sold information that would get someone killed (as far as anyone can prove), never used his network for anything other than knowing. But the network exists. The files exist. And Merrick is mortal — someday, someone will inherit that network. The succession question keeps the other council members awake at night.

## Hook

Merrick's Hollowed informant has gone silent — three weeks with no contact. This has never happened before. Merrick is genuinely concerned — not for the informant's safety, but because a silent informant means something is happening in the Hollows that even the Hollowed don't understand. He's willing to share information with anyone who can find out what.

# Lord Aldric Voss

Lord Voss is the wealthiest and most powerful member of the Thornwall Council — and the most vocal opponent of Riftborn integration. He controls the farmland surrounding Thornwall, the grain supply, and the livestock trade. His family has held their council seat for seven generations. He believes, with genuine conviction, that he is protecting the Severed Lands from a threat.

Voss is not a villain in his own mind. He's a patriarch who's watched Rift surges coincide with Riftborn arrivals for his entire life. He's seen the Hollowed — people he knew, people he grew up with — transformed into something unrecognizable. He's buried friends who were killed by riftbeasts that didn't exist before the Rift started spreading. He's drawn a conclusion: Riftborn are connected to the Rift, the Rift is destroying the world, therefore Riftborn are dangerous. It's not malice. It's a lifetime of evidence pointing in one direction, and no one has ever shown him evidence pointing anywhere else.

His son died six years ago — killed by a Rift surge while traveling the eastern route. Voss doesn't talk about it. His politics did.

## Personality

Voss is formal, deliberate, and used to being obeyed. He doesn't shout. He doesn't need to. When Lord Voss speaks in council, the room goes quiet — not because he's intimidating, but because he's been right often enough that people listen. He treats opposition with patience rather than hostility — he believes his position is correct and that time will prove it. This makes him more dangerous than a rabid zealot. A zealot can be dismissed. Voss can't.

He genuinely believes Riftborn are victims as much as threats — souls displaced by the Rift, deserving of compassion, but too dangerous to integrate into settled society. He advocates for "assisted settlement" — designated Riftborn zones, supervised travel, regulated trade. He doesn't see this as oppression. He sees it as protection.

## Role in a Campaign

**As antagonist:** Voss is the face of institutional anti-Riftborn sentiment. He pushes for registration requirements, travel restrictions, and segregation policies. He's not the final boss — he's the obstacle that makes every Riftborn's life harder. A campaign that aligns with the Returners or the Stayers will clash with Voss repeatedly.

**As potential ally:** Voss is not unreachable. Evidence that Riftborn arrivals don't cause surges — or that something else is accelerating the Doors' decline — could shift his position. He's a man who follows evidence, even when that evidence contradicts his conclusions. A campaign that presents him with proof he can't dismiss might turn an enemy into an uncertain ally. He won't apologize. He will change his vote.

## Behind the Screen

Voss's anti-Riftborn policies are genuine, but they're also politically useful. Keeping Riftborn marginalized keeps the Warrens contained, keeps the Returners at Waystation, keeps Thornwall's settled population comfortable. Voss doesn't think of it this way — but his politics and his power are mutually reinforcing, and he's never had to examine that too closely. A campaign that forces him to confront the consequences of his policies — the lives destroyed, the families separated — might break him. Or it might make him double down.

# Castellan Voss

Castellan Voss is the Knight-Commander of the Warden Lodge — no relation to Thornwall's House Voss, a fact he mentions frequently and with visible irritation. He's led the Lodge for fifteen years, training knights in Warden combat techniques and overseeing the Echo Dice bonding rituals that are the Lodge's signature discipline.

Voss is a warrior-historian. He believes that understanding the Wardens means practicing what they practiced — not just studying their inscriptions, but moving like they moved, fighting like they fought, thinking like they thought. His knights learn Warden combat forms alongside Warden history. The two are inseparable. You can't understand a people's fighting style without understanding why they fought.

The Lodge's artifact vault contains the largest collection of bonded Warden weapons in the Severed Lands. Voss has bonded with three of them — a sword, a shield, and a gauntlet that he never removes. He says the Wardens speak through their artifacts, if you listen. He says the sword is the most talkative.

## Personality

Voss is stern, direct, and unexpectedly warm with his knights. He treats the Lodge as family — dysfunctional, argumentative, fiercely loyal family. He knows every knight's name, every squire's background, every smith's specialty. He attends every bonding ritual personally. He writes the condolence letters when a knight falls.

He's also dying. A Rift-touched lung condition, contracted during an expedition into the deep Cairnfields. His healers give him a year, maybe two. He hasn't told the Lodge. He's trying to prepare them for succession without them realizing he's preparing them for succession.

Voss's successor must be elected by the sworn knights. Two candidates have emerged: a traditionalist who wants to preserve the Lodge's methods, and a reformer who wants to train more knights faster. The vote is in three months. Voss is trying to stay alive long enough to see it through — and trying not to let either candidate realize how little time he has left.

# Joss

Joss is a prospector — one of the independent scavengers who work the Cairnfields without crew affiliation, guild membership, or any backup beyond their own wits. They've been doing this for twelve years. They're still alive. That's statistically remarkable.

Joss specializes in Warden fragments — the smaller pieces that the crews overlook, the shards embedded in pillar walls, the fragments that surface after Rift surges. They're not looking for the big score. They're looking for consistent finds, enough to keep them supplied and moving. They know the Cairnfields' lesser-known routes — the pillar paths the Raiders don't patrol, the pools the riftbeasts have abandoned.

Joss will guide anyone for a price. They'll also leave anyone behind if the situation gets too dangerous. They're upfront about this. "I'm a guide, not a hero" is their standard contract opener. Clients appreciate the honesty. Some of them still hire Joss. Some of them don't come back.

## Personality

Joss is pragmatic, self-interested, and refreshingly honest about both. They don't pretend to be brave. They don't pretend to be noble. They're a prospector trying to make a living in the most dangerous place in the Severed Lands. Everything else is marketing.

# Doctor Cipher

Doctor Cipher was the head of the Athenaeum's School of Rift Dynamics before she was expelled for deliberately Hollowing a volunteer to study the progression. She argues that the volunteer consented, that the data was invaluable, that the Athenaeum's ethics are cowardice disguised as caution. She's not wrong about any of those things. She's also not someone you should trust with anything you care about.

Cipher runs the Unbound — the scattered community of expelled scholars and forbidden researchers — from a makeshift laboratory in the Hollows. Her current project is a device she calls the Pool Stabilizer: a Warden-derived mechanism that she claims can control a Rift pool, turning it from a hazard into a controllable energy source. Her previous three prototypes exploded. The fourth is almost ready.

Cipher is brilliant, charismatic, and utterly convinced of her own righteousness. She genuinely believes that the Athenaeum's restrictions are holding back research that could save lives — stabilize Door sites, reverse Hollowing, maybe even close the Rift entirely. She might be right. She might be building a bomb.

## Personality

Cipher treats ethics as an engineering problem. Every moral objection is a constraint to be optimized around, not a line to be respected. She's not evil — she genuinely wants to help people. She just believes that the ends justify any means, and she's very good at convincing others of the same.

She's charming in a way that's hard to resist. She listens. She validates concerns. She explains her reasoning in terms that make perfect sense until you're no longer in the room with her and suddenly the logic doesn't hold. Her former colleagues describe her as "the most dangerous person I've ever respected."

## Hook

Cipher's Pool Stabilizer is ready for a full test. She needs a Rift pool large enough to matter — one of the major pools in the Hollows or the Deep Rift in the Cairnfields. She's recruiting escorts. She's also recruiting subjects to stand near the pool during activation, "in case of unexpected resonance." The pay is generous. The risk is absolute.

# The Mirror

The Mirror is a fortune-teller in the Crossroads — a Riftborn in the early stages of Hollowing, whose violet-flecked eyes supposedly see fragments of possible futures. Her readings are practical: will the caravan arrive safely, should I take the contract, is my missing relative still alive. The answers aren't always what people want. They're usually what they needed to hear.

The Athenaeum has studied her. The Hollowed consider her barely Touched — a beginner, not a true practitioner. The Mirror doesn't care about either assessment. She's running a business. The Veil provides. She interprets. The customers pay.

## Personality

The Mirror is theatrical, shrewd, and surprisingly honest about her own limitations. She'll tell you when she's guessing. She'll tell you when she's sure. She'll tell you when the answer scares her. The honesty is part of the performance. The performance is part of the truth.

Gareth was a Thornwall guard captain for twelve years before he was discharged for "excessive ruthlessness" in a bandit crackdown. The council's official finding: he executed prisoners. Gareth is a man who believes the world is harsh and that pretending otherwise gets people killed. He's not sadistic — he's pragmatic to the point of brutality. He respects courage and competence. He despises weakness and hypocrisy. The Thornwall Council, in his view, is full of both.

He's a villain in the council's eyes and a folk hero in the Warrens — the guard captain who turned on his masters. Gareth doesn't care about either reputation. He cares about running his band, following the code, and making enough coin to keep his people fed through the winter.

## Hook

Gareth has called a moot — a gathering of all Jackal bands. He wants to unite them into a single organization under his command. Half the bands support him. # The Prophet of Four Corners

# Vesper

Vesper is the Athenaeum's head librarian — the keeper of the Severed Lands' largest collection of pre-Rift and Warden texts. She's been at the Athenaeum for thirty years, and she's read more of the collection than anyone alive. She knows which shelves hold the dangerous material. # Orin Thatch

Orin Thatch is the Route Warden of the Caravaneers' Guild — the elected representative of the Severed Lands' independent merchants. He's been running the southern route for twenty years, surviving three Jackal raids, two riftbeast attacks, and one marriage that ended amicably enough that they still trade together.

# Salt-Ash

Salt-Ash was a scholar of Hollowed consciousness at the Athenaeum before she became her own research subject. She was studying the cognitive effects of Rift exposure when she realized she'd been exposed herself — slow, cumulative, the result of years working with Rift-touched materials without adequate protection. By the time she noticed, her eyes were already violet.

She joined the Unbound rather than retreating into the depths. Salt-Ash is a Speaker — her speech fragments, her perceptions blur between what's real and what the Rift shows her — but her research continues. She takes notes in a script that only other Hollowed can read. The notes are brilliant. They're also the most comprehensive study of Hollowed cognition ever produced. The Athenaeum would pay anything for access. Salt-Ash won't sell.

She's been translating Warden inscriptions that the Athenaeum couldn't crack. The Hollowed see the script differently — the Rift reveals layers of meaning that the unexposed miss. What she's found: a Warden warning, repeated across multiple Door sites. "The last Door must not open." She's not sure if it's a warning that the last Door shouldn't open, or a warning about what happens if it does.

## Personality

Salt-Ash is intense, fragmented, and fighting to stay coherent. The Hollowing is progressive — she knows she's losing language, losing linear thought, losing the ability to distinguish between research and revelation. She's racing her own deterioration, trying to finish her work before the Hollowing finishes her.

# Sister Iron

Sister Iron is the founder of the Anchor Church — the Severed Lands' youngest and fastest-growing faith. She was a Thornwall blacksmith before she touched a dormant Door fragment thirty years ago and experienced what she describes as a revelation. The fragment spoke to her — not in words, but in certainty. The Doors exist to provide a way home. Not just for Riftborn. For everyone.

Iron founded the Church on that certainty. For thirty years, she's preached that the Doors are sacred, the Wardens were prophets, and the Rift is a trial — a crucible preparing the faithful for something on the other side. Her congregation has grown from a handful of Riftborn in a Nexus basement to hundreds across three settlements. She's old now — her hands shake, her voice cracks when she preaches too long. But the certainty is undimmed. If anything, it's stronger.

Iron has never claimed to speak for the Doors. She says she only repeats what they told her. The fact that no one else has heard the Doors speak is, she says, because no one else has listened properly. This claim is either profound or delusional. Iron doesn't care which.

## Personality

Iron is gentle, patient, and utterly immovable. She doesn't argue — she witnesses. She doesn't persuade — she describes what she experienced and lets the listener decide. This makes her nearly impossible to debate. You can't argue with someone's revelation. You can only decide whether you believe them.

She's aware that the Church is growing faster than she can guide it. She's aware that some of her followers — the Revealers — want to be more militant. She's resisted them, but she's old, and she won't be here forever. The question of succession frightens her more than she admits.

## Role in a Campaign

**As ally:** Iron is a source of spiritual guidance, a safe harbor for Riftborn characters, and a moral counterweight to V's secular pragmatism. Where V offers research, Iron offers faith. A campaign can draw on both.

**As antagonist:** If the Revealers seize control of the Church — or if Iron's certainty hardens into fanaticism — the Anchor Church could become an obstacle. A faith that believes the Doors must open at any cost is not so different from the Radicals. Iron would resist that path. She might not succeed.

## Hook

Iron has announced that the Doors will speak again — within the year. She doesn't know to whom or where. She only knows what the fragment told her. Every faction is watching. Some are already positioning to be the recipient. Some are positioning to prevent it.

# The Inkwell

The Inkwell was an Athenaeum cartographer expelled for Hoarding — the institution's term for withholding findings. They discovered a map of Warden Door sites that didn't match any known configuration. Instead of sharing it, they disappeared into the Hollows. They've been mapping ever since — not just the Severed Lands, but what lies beneath them.

The Inkwell is Hollowed now — Speaker stage. Their speech is a mix of coherent sentences and Rift-fragments. Their maps are drawn in a hand that shakes when the phasing is close and steadies when it passes. The maps are the most accurate cartography of the Hollows in existence. They're also deeply unsettling. Some of the locations on them don't exist. Yet.

The Inkwell surfaced recently in the Thornwall market, selling maps. They looked terrible — thin, hollow-eyed, hands trembling. They wouldn't discuss what they found in the deep Hollows. They just kept saying the maps were accurate and the price was fair. Someone asked about a route marked in red. The Inkwell said that route didn't go anywhere you'd want to visit. Then they packed up and left.

## Personality

The Inkwell is distracted, brilliant, and increasingly difficult to communicate with. The Hollowing is progressing — they lose track of conversations, respond to things no one else said, stare at empty corners for minutes at a time. But their maps remain flawless. Whatever the Rift is showing them, it's real. The question is whether the Inkwell is mapping the Hollows or something the Hollows is becoming.

# The Silent

The Silent is a Rememberer who took a vow of silence — not as penance, but as witness. They believe that if they stop speaking, they can hear the names better. Decades into the vow, they're certain they were right.

The Silent communicates through writing — a small slate and chalk, always at hand. Their handwriting is precise, unhurried. They treat every written response as if it's the only thing they'll say all day. Sometimes it is. Their ledger is written in a script no one can read, but when they recite the names — silently, lips moving, eyes closed — the effect is the same as any other Rememberer's recitation. Something about it feels sacred.

The Silent appears where Riftborn are in danger. They don't announce themselves. They don't stay afterward. They arrive, they help, they write a few names in their ledger, and they leave. No one knows how they know where to go. The Silent doesn't explain.

## Personality

The Silent is patient, watchful, and impossible to read. Their silence isn't cold — they smile, they nod, they express warmth through gesture and expression. But the silence is absolute. They haven't spoken in decades. They don't intend to start now.

## Hook

The Silent has been seen near Thornwall — unusual, they rarely come this far east. They've been watching the council hall. They've been writing names. Someone on the council is in danger. The Silent is waiting.

# Vale

Vale guides people through the Undercroft — the network of pre-Rift tunnels and catacombs beneath Nexus. They know the routes that connect to the Hollows (officially denied, universally known), the passages the Athenaeum uses for secure storage (officially denied, functionally mapped), and the places where the Undercroft gets... strange.

The price varies — coin for standard routes, favors for dangerous ones, and "you don't want to know" for the routes that go deep enough to touch the Hollows. No one's ever taken that last option. ## Personality

# Reef

Reef is a Verdant Scaled hunter — young by Scaled standards, which means she's been hunting the Margin for twenty years. She's one of the few Scaled who regularly interacts with outsiders, serving as a guide for Returner patrols and the occasional Guild caravan that needs to cross Margin territory.

Reef speaks Common with an accent that makes everything sound like a question. She finds outsiders confusing — their urgency, their impatience, their need to be somewhere by a specific time. The Margin doesn't care about schedules. Reef has learned to translate between Margin-time and outsider-time, but it's clearly an effort.

She guides because Tide-Mother asked her to — the Elders decided that the Scaled needed a bridge to the outside world, and Reef drew the short straw. She doesn't resent it. She's just not sure why it matters. The Margin provides everything the Scaled need. Everything beyond the Margin is someone else's problem.

## Personality

Reef is patient, observant, and bemused by outsiders. She treats escort missions like babysitting — keep the outsiders alive, keep them on the clearings, don't let them touch anything that glows. She's very good at it. She'd rather be hunting.

# Tide-Mother

Tide-Mother is the oldest Verdant Scaled alive — a reptilian Riftborn who's been hunting the Verdant Margin for over sixty years. Her scales are scarred with Rift-burns that glow faintly in the dark, each one a record of a riftbeast kill. She's killed three Elder Riftbeasts. The youngest Scaled hunters tell stories about her. The stories don't do her justice.

She leads the Scaled not by authority but by consensus. When the Scale-Elders meet at the Heartwood, Tide-Mother speaks rarely. When she does speak, the other Elders stop talking. Her voice is quiet — a rasp, damaged by decades of Rift exposure — but it carries. The Scaled have learned that when Tide-Mother has something to say, it's because she's already considered every angle and reached the only conclusion worth reaching.

## Personality

Tide-Mother is patient in a way that unsettles non-Scaled. She measures time in seasons, not days. A conversation that takes an hour doesn't bother her — she's been in the Margin for sixty years. An hour is nothing. She treats outsiders with caution but not hostility. The Scaled have no interest in the politics of the settled lands, but they're not isolationists. They watch. They wait. They hunt.

She carries a Rift-touched spear that's absorbed the energy of every riftbeast it's killed. The spear hums when riftbeasts are near. It sings when Elder Riftbeasts are near. Tide-Mother holds it loosely, like an old friend.

## Hook

Tide-Mother has requested a meeting with the Returners — something she hasn't done in twenty years. The Margin is changing. The growth is accelerating. Something is feeding the Rift pools, and she doesn't know what. She's willing to grant outsiders access to the deep canopy — something the Scaled have never done — in exchange for answers.

# The Archivist

The Archivist claims to be the last of her order — a Veil-touched Elf who's been maintaining the Archivist's Spire for longer than anyone can verify. The Spire is a tower in the Hollows that leans at an impossible angle but never falls, its interior filled with pre-Rift books, most too degraded to read, some in languages that don't exist.

She trades information for Warden fragments — a book consulted for a shard of Door stone, a translation provided for a sigil-stone. Her rates are consistent. Her knowledge is vast. Her patience for scholars who ask the wrong questions is nonexistent. She's been known to eject visitors who waste her time. The Spire's front door opens onto a different street each time, so "ejecting" someone is a serious threat.

The Archivist is Hollowed — Speaker stage, violet eyes, speech that fragments when she's tired. She's been in the Hollows for decades, maybe centuries. Time works differently in the Spire. She stopped counting years a long time ago.

## Personality

The Archivist is imperious, precise, and carrying a sadness she doesn't discuss. The Spire is her life's work. The books are her responsibility. She'll be here until the last page crumbles, and she's made peace with that.

# The Glass Monk

The Glass Monk is what happens when a phase-step goes wrong. They were a promising Veiled Path practitioner, years into their training, when a misjudged step through the Veil left them partially phased — their body permanently caught between reality and the Rift. They're partially transparent now. Their footsteps make no sound. Their voice, when they speak, is barely audible — a whisper at the edge of hearing.

They can't teach anymore. The phase-step technique requires physical contact to demonstrate, and the Glass Monk's touch is... wrong. Cold. Faint. Like touching something through water. Students who've tried to learn from them report nightmares that last for weeks.

The Glass Monk serves as the Veiled Path's living warning: the Veil takes as much as it gives. They've accepted this role with a grace that surprises everyone. They live near the Spire, keeping Old Crane company when Crane wants company and leaving him alone when he doesn't. They speak rarely. When they do, it's worth hearing.

## Personality

The Glass Monk is calm, accepting, and deeply sad. They don't regret their training. They regret the mistake that ended it. They've made peace with being a warning rather than a teacher. It's not the legacy they wanted. It's the one they have.

# War-Captain Korr

War-Captain Korr leads the Ashen Claw — the largest and most aggressive Rift Raider warband in the Cairnfields. He arrived through the Rift mid-battle, an entire company of soldiers pulled from their war-world into the Severed Lands. He never stopped fighting.

Korr is a strategist, not a brute. His raids are coordinated, his targets are chosen for maximum disruption, and he's been studying Thornwall's guard rotations for months. He knows the Cairnfields better than the Returners do. He knows the trade routes better than the Jackals do. He's been planning something — not just raiding, but something larger. The other warbands are starting to wonder what.

Korr communicates through Rift-tongue, which no outsider speaks, and through the Rift Seekers who occasionally serve as unwilling translators. When he deigns to address outsiders directly, he speaks Common with an accent that sounds like grinding stone. His words are precise. He doesn't waste them.

## Personality

Korr is not cruel, but he is absolute. He believes the Rift brought his people here for a purpose — to continue the Eternal Battle on new ground. He doesn't hate the settled folk or the Returners. He simply categorizes them as combatants, and he treats combatants as targets.

He respects strength. A party that fights well might earn his acknowledgment — not his friendship, but his recognition as worthy opponents. A party that negotiates from a position of strength might earn a temporary truce. A party that shows weakness will be raided.

## Behind the Screen

Korr has information about the missing Anchor Doors — something his scouts found in the deep Cairnfields. He's sent a message to Waystation requesting a meeting with V. What he wants in exchange, and whether he's negotiating in good faith, is up to the DM. He might be a warlord seeking legitimacy. He might be a soldier who's found something that scares even him.

# War-Captain Vex

War-Captain Vex leads the Silent Wing — the Rift Raider warband that specializes in aerial attacks. Her raiders ride tamed Rift Pteranodons, diving from pillar-tops onto caravans and patrols below. The Silent Wing is the most disciplined warband in the Cairnfields, trained to execute complex aerial maneuvers without verbal communication.

Vex hasn't spoken in years. A Rift surge destroyed her voice during a raid on a Returner patrol — not killing her, but burning something out of her throat. She communicates through hand signals and written orders. Her warband has adapted completely. The Silent Wing operates in total silence during raids — no shouted commands, no battle cries, just the shriek of pteranodons and the impact of steel.

Vex is Korr's most reliable ally — and his biggest potential rival. The Ashen Claw is the largest warband, but the Silent Wing is the most feared. Vex is silent, observant, and absolutely certain of her own competence. She communicates through action rather than words. retained_styles.name: Severed Lands K: anime illustration
retained_styles.brief:
Draw original heroic fantasy characters with a clearly anime foundation and a controlled painted
finish. Use the supplied style image to judge drawing, edge control and shading. Each subject's
own references determine identity, age, species, build, complexion, hair and costume.

Faces: construct a deliberate stylized face with clean cheek/jaw silhouettes and readable eye
shapes. Give the upper eyelid a confident dark edge; design the iris, pupil and small catchlight
as graphic shapes. Make brows and mouth economical expressive marks. Describe the nose through
a small designed contour and broad light/shadow shapes. Keep the face recognizable through
shape and expression, with restrained surface detail.

Age and anatomy: retain the actual subject's age, proportions and distinctive features. Older
anime faces use mature silhouettes and a few intentional age lines; children retain their own
proportions. Scars keep their established side and shape. Species and creatures retain their
authored anatomy. The reference character's youth, face and body are never a template for others.

Hair: design large interlocking locks and ribbon-like groups with a clear silhouette. Use
selective interior lines, curved highlights and a few flyaways to explain those groups. Preserve
the subject's own cut, colour and hair texture; braids, curls and cropped hair remain distinct.

Shading: begin with broad, intentional shadow shapes that keep the drawing legible. Use controlled
soft transitions within those shapes to give painted depth; keep key facial and hair edges crisp.
Warm ivory key light and cool coloured shadows support the drawing. Keep skin smooth at normal
viewing size, with age marks chosen deliberately. Surface grain, pores, dirt and scratches are
secondary local details rather than a finish covering the entire face or costume.

Colour: preserve distinct local colours and the subject's natural complexion. Pale linen reads
as pale linen; charcoal, plum, olive and auburn remain distinguishable under the same light.
Use coloured shadows and selective accents to keep dark fantasy readable. Restrict amber light
to illuminated planes instead of washing every material in a bronze filter. Never borrow the
style character's skin or hair colour to achieve the match.

Materials: explain cloth folds, leather seams and metal edges with selected shapes and highlights.
Place texture where it describes a particular material or authored wear. Ornament belongs to
the subject's established design. A cook's apron and a guard's practical uniform receive the same
careful illustration as a scholar's cape without gaining its embroidery, jewellery or silhouette.

Composition: give the subject a clear silhouette and character-appropriate expression. Keep
complete heads, hair and equipment inside usable margins. Portraits retain recognizable eyes,
face shape and expression at small UI sizes. Plain dark grounds suit reference studies; actual
environment and lighting follow the requested asset. The final image must retain the benchmark's
anime drawing even when its colour, age, species or clothing is very different.
